abstract: CAR T-cell infusion products are commonly characterized in terms of their cellular populations and transcriptional programs, but these descriptions do not fully capture how a product is organized as a system. We analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data from the infusion products of 163 patients across eight cohorts to investigate how system-level transcriptional organization relates to both clinical outcome and how cellular features vary together across patients. For each patient, we constructed a gene-dependency graph using mutual information between the binary detection states of each gene pair across infusion cells. To characterize each patient's network architecture, we define spectral organization, O{lambda}, a measure of the relative persistence of collective patterns of gene dependence in the network. Using hierarchical Bayesian survival models, we assessed the associations of both O{lambda} and various established cellular features with treatment outcome. Higher spectral organization was associated with a higher hazard of treatment failure in both a continuous model (hazard ratio per standard deviation, 1.45, 95% credible interval 1.07-2.19) and a smooth transition model (hazard ratio comparing the high and low regimes, 2.03, 95% credible interval 1.10-3.53). When we investigated how cellular features covary across patients, we found that correlations among both T-cell programs and cell type proportions aligned more coherently with treatment failure risk in the high O{lambda} regime compared to the low regime, revealing a systems-level pattern that helps explain the clinical relevance of spectral organization. Gene set enrichment analysis further showed that more persistent architectures were associated with inflammation and cellular interaction pathways, whereas lower spectral organization was associated with biosynthetic and genome maintenance pathways, consistent with the hypothesis that the organizational state of an infusion product reflects its capacity to reconfigure in response to CAR T treatment. Altogether, our findings identify spectral organization as a property of the infusion product as a whole that connects gene-dependency architecture within individual products to the collective variation of cellular features across patients. This framework therefore motivates studying CAR T biology from a systems perspective alongside established descriptions of cellular state.
